edges: Dolin says the Civil War’s collapse of northern demand came as kerosene became the illuminant of choice.
Bockstoce reads the decline of sperm oil’s price under substitute illuminants as what pushed whalers toward the Arctic baleen.
The Shenandoah’s Arctic cruise and the 1871 disaster both fall in the same decline of the American fleet.
Mège’s suet process is the margarine process of the patent.
Jurgens bought the process and patent in 1871 and made margarine at scale.
Van Stuyvenberg ties Germany’s Margarine Act to the anti-margarine campaign provoked by margarine’s growth.
Van Stuyvenberg ties the 1886 federal law to the dairy lobby’s campaign against the new fat.
Much cottonseed oil went into oleomargarine, as Mueller says.
Cronon’s packers made oleomargarine and stearin in their laboratories from the 1880s.
The federal act followed the state bans and their failure, as van Stuyvenberg relates.
German protection and the margarine boom set up the dairy backlash that led to the 1887 Act.
Twain’s fake butter and bogus oil are the cottonseed and margarine economy seen by a contemporary.
Industrial demand for soap, candles and cheap margarine drove the palm-kernel trade.
Law ties Old Calabar’s kernel exports to Lever’s kernel-and-coconut soap.
Lever’s Sunlight and P&G’s Ivory are the two great branded soaps of the 1880s, as Ward and Dyer tell.
The island famine is the cost to Arctic hunters of the same whaling that the bowhead fishery reports as a bonanza.
The Western restaurants of the Meiji years serve the meat and fat that the campaign of 1872 made fashionable.
The Sydney office is an arm of Lever Brothers, whose Port Sunlight works need the copra and tallow it sends home.
Pacific copra in Sydney and the palm-kernel trade of West Africa feed the same soap kettles.
The Japan Grounds and the Arctic were fished by the same American whaling fleet.
Kiple has Europe’s peanut-oil mills drawing first on West Africa and then, after the Suez Canal, on India.
